name: git worktrees and tmux
title: Ninebrains vs running git worktrees and tmux yourself
description: Do you need a tool to run coding agents in parallel, or are git worktree and tmux enough? What Ninebrains adds on top, and when the manual setup is the better choice.
summary: Maximum composability, nothing to install. You build the plan and the checks yourself.
answer: You can run Claude Code or Codex in parallel with nothing but git worktree and tmux, and for a power user who wants full control that is often enough. Ninebrains does the worktrees and panes for you, then adds what the manual setup lacks: a job graph with dependencies, a mailbox between lanes, and checks that must pass before work counts as done.
note: Here the other column describes git and tmux themselves. Anything a manual setup has beyond them is whatever you script yourself.

what.text: git worktree lets one repository check out more than one branch at a time, each in its own working tree. tmux is a terminal multiplexer.

licence.text: git is free and open source.

isolation.text: One working tree per branch, sharing one repository.

chooseThem.text: You want maximum composability and already live in tmux: git worktree add plus a pane per agent is a few commands.
You want nothing new installed and nothing between you and the agents’ terminals.

chooseUs: You want the worktrees, branches, terminals and cleanup handled for you, with a grid that shows each agent’s status.
You want a plan that knows which job depends on which, and hands ready jobs to idle agents.
You want a second run, with read-only tools in a disposable checkout, to check the work before you read it.

faq.q: Do git worktrees prevent merge conflicts between agents?
faq.a: No. Worktrees stop agents overwriting each other’s files at the same time. Two branches can still conflict when you merge them, and neither git nor Ninebrains removes that.
